title: Moore legislation to clarify vaccine guidelines adds to ‘confusion’ instead, opponents say
summary: The Moore administration's plan to counteract "confusion" over shifting federal vaccine recommendations by granting more authority to state officials will just create more confusion, not less, critics told a Senate committee Tuesday.
content:
by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters February 10, 2026

by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters February 10, 2026

The Moore administration’s plan to counteract “confusion” over shifting federal vaccine recommendations by granting more authority to state officials will just create more confusion, not less, critics told a Senate committee Tuesday.

“It is unnecessarily confusing for the parents of our state, and it is contributing to the politicization of all health care policy,” Catherine Garrett, who leads a patient advocacy group called Love Maryland, said in virtual testimony to the Senate Finance Committee.

Garrett was testifying against Senate Bill 385, the so-called Vax Act, that would grant that state health secretary the authority to set vaccine recommendations for Marylanders, independent of any federal guidelines. The bill is priority legislation for Gov. Wes Moore (D), who announced it last month shortly after U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. began watering down vaccine recommendations.

In January, President Donald Trump (R) issued a memorandum directing Kennedy and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to reevaluate childhood vaccines based on “best practices from peer, developed countries.” The CDC then announced it was reducing the number of vaccinations recommended for all children.

Now, vaccinations protecting children against rotavirus, influenza, COVID-19 and hepatitis A and B are recommended only for those with severe health complications, or after consultation with a health care provider. Previously, the vaccinations were broadly recommended for all children.

Under the Vax Act, Maryland Health Secretary Meena Seshamani would be able to consider federal guidance when issuing vaccination recommendations for the state. But the bill places more emphasis on the recommendations of major medical societies and organizations, such as the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Academy of Family Physicians.

The bill would also grant the secretary authority to set recommendations for screenings and preventative services. Many state laws involving insurance coverage are currently tied to recommendations issued by federal agencies such as the CDC or the Food and Drug Administration.

The recent disconnect between federal health authorities and medical organizations has led to public confusion over vaccine safety and best practices. Seshamani and other state officials hope the Vax Act will work to restore confidence in the effectiveness of vaccines.

Seshamani told lawmakers the legislation would not issue vaccine requirements but would keep vaccines available for those who want them by ensuring they’re covered by insurance companies, regardless of decisions made at federal agencies.

“This legislation does not create any mandates,” Seshamani said. “What this legislation does say is that the secretary can have recommendations for vaccines — and that translates to what commercial insurance should cover at no cost sharing and what pharmacists are then able to administer at the pharmacy.”

Sen. Benjamin Kramer (D-Montgomery) asked Seshamani if the legislation was a response to “the non-science-based, irresponsible lunacy coming from our tinfoil-hat wearing” HHS secretary, a noted vaccine skeptic.

Seshamani did not respond to the senator’s characterization of Kennedy, but told the Finance Committee that confusion around vaccines “is palpable.”

“I think it is very important that we in the state are able to provide to our families as they are making decisions with their doctors and other clinicians, and that we remove any financial barriers that could exist to being able to get the care that people need,” Seshasmani said.

But Annapolis resident Jenna Butler is not convinced.

“I can tell you as a parent, talking with parents, this bill does nothing to restore confidence,” Butler said, testifying virtually.

Maryland advocates hope new multistate public health coalition will clarify vaccine ‘confusion’

Sarah Cusack, called the Vax Act unnecessary — an assertion echoed by Senate Minority Leader Steve Hershey (R-Upper Shore) and Minority Whip Justin Ready (R-Carroll and Frederick).

The Moore administration already took steps to ensure insurance companies cover vaccines that were recommended prior to recent changes under the Trump administration. In addition, the Vax Act does not require anyone to get a specific vaccine, and Seshamani assured that individuals make decisions for themselves in consultation with their doctors.

Cusack argued that the end goals of the state legislation reflect new federal guidance.

“I actually think that the Vax Act is doing the same thing that the federal government did,” Cusack said. “The (federal) government reclassified some vaccinations as clinical decision-making, meaning that the parent and the patient work with the physician. And that’s actually what the Vax Act is doing. There are no mandates — it says you should work with your physician and make decisions.”

Sen. Clarence Lam (D-Anne Arundel and Howard) believes that the Trump administration has “turned their back on science” and “installed a sloppy, slapped together process led by the stooges of RFK Jr.”

“This is something that is certainly needed,” Lam said of the Vax Act, “because we had a gold standard process that was set up by the federal government, led by the CDC, that has been gutted and made a mockery of across the country.”

A companion measure in the House, House Bill 637, is scheduled for a hearing Feb. 26 before the House Health Committee.
